title: Self-Driving Cars Have An Aging Problem
gist: Continuous edge-AI inference in software-defined vehicles is turning automotive electronics from intermittent-duty into always-on parts, accelerating sensor and silicon aging in ways nobody has a decade of data for. Executives from Rambus, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, Keysight, Imagination Technologies, Arm and Infineon argue this forces on-chip aging monitors, fleet-wide degradation modeling, GPU-style programmable headroom, SoC-wide ASIL certification, and a new class of security risk where analog drift becomes an attack surface.

themes.theme: Always-on inference as an aging accelerant

insights.claim: Software-defined vehicles run continuous AI inference for perception, sensor fusion, driver monitoring and autonomous functions, replacing the intermittent duty cycles that traditional automotive electronics were qualified against and materially shortening component life.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Automotive silicon reliability budgets written for intermittent operation are structurally optimistic; watch for warranty-reserve and recall risk at OEMs shipping L2+/L3 stacks on legacy qualification assumptions.
insights.quote: As AI is ‘always on,’ it contributes to the gradual decline of the hardware within automotive systems
insights.locator: AI impact on sensor health, aging

insights.claim: Four specific mechanisms drive AI-accelerated automotive aging: higher average die temperature from sustained compute, continuous electrical stress on transistors, loss of thermal recovery periods because processors and sensors are rarely idle, and long-term drift in analog components and sensor calibration.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist for stress-testing any automotive AI silicon story — vendors that only address thermals are covering one of four failure vectors.
insights.quote: higher average temperatures from sustained compute workloads, continuous electrical stress on transistors, reduced thermal recovery periods because processors and sensors are rarely idle
insights.locator: The integration of AI into cars

insights.claim: Cameras, radar, lidar and the chips processing their data now remain active throughout the entire duration of vehicle operation, so the sensor stack — not just the compute SoC — carries the incremental aging load from AI workloads.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Sensor suppliers, not only SoC vendors, face the replacement/service-life question — a cost line automakers have not obviously priced into robotaxi unit economics.
insights.locator: Sensors like cameras, radar, lidar

insights.claim: Safety-critical vehicle systems are expected to last a decade or more, yet the workload they see varies with how often, how aggressively and where a vehicle is driven, plus the corner cases it randomly encounters — meaning identical hardware will age along widely dispersed curves.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Aging is a distribution, not a number; any warranty or remaining-useful-life model built on a fleet average will understate tail risk in high-utilization fleets like robotaxis and delivery.
insights.locator: Safety-critical systems in vehicles are expected

insights.claim: AI workloads in vehicles will keep intensifying as more autonomy is added, so the aging problem is compounding rather than one-time — hardware fielded today faces heavier inference loads later in its life than at deployment.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Over-the-air feature upgrades quietly transfer stress onto already-aged silicon; an OTA-heavy roadmap is a hidden reliability liability.
insights.locator: These automotive AI workloads are only going to get more strenuous

themes.theme: Day-one safety stats vs. lifetime validation

insights.claim: A just-released Insurance Institute for Highway Safety report found Waymo's L4 vehicles had 68% fewer reportable crashes than human drivers and a 91% lower rate of rear-ending another vehicle.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: The strongest third-party safety validation yet for L4 — supportive for AV insurance-cost arguments and for regulatory expansion of driverless permits.
insights.quote: Waymo’s L4 vehicles experienced 68% fewer reportable crashes than human drivers, and a 91% lower rate of rear-ending another vehicle
insights.locator: A just-released report by the Insurance Institute

insights.claim: No solid data exists for how autonomous-vehicle crash rates shift over a decade of operation, because the technology is too new — every published AV safety statistic is effectively a measurement of young, un-aged hardware.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: The bull case for AV safety rests on day-one data; a degradation-driven regression in a mature fleet is an unpriced tail risk for AV operators and their insurers.
insights.quote: But the technology is so new that no solid data exists for how and where those rates might shift over the course of a decade.
insights.locator: But the technology is so new

insights.claim: Automotive companies and their suppliers are pouring tens of billions of dollars into autonomous driving while fundamental questions about when supplying sensors degrade, how AI models handle that aging, and how to size systems for future AI scaling remain unresolved.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Capital is committed ahead of the reliability science — favors suppliers selling monitoring, test and lifecycle-analytics tooling into a problem the industry must retrofit.
insights.locator: Automotive companies and their suppliers are pouring

insights.claim: The article's closing thesis is that automakers, chipmakers and AI developers must treat aging, adaptability and security as one interconnected design problem, validating systems not for day-one performance but for how safely they can evolve across a vehicle's lifetime.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: The unifying frame for the piece: lifetime-evolution validation is the next major cost and tooling category in automotive semis, spanning EDA, test, security IP and simulation.
insights.quote: That means validating systems not just for how they perform on day one, but for how safely they can evolve over a vehicle’s lifetime.
insights.locator: Conclusion

themes.theme: One fleet model vs. individually aging sensors

insights.claim: Each individual sensor ages differently, and no two sensors degrade the same way, so degradation cannot be handled by a single deterministic compensation curve.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Per-unit calibration drift means field-return diagnostics and per-vehicle health telemetry become mandatory, expanding the addressable market for in-field analytics.
insights.quote: There won’t be two sensors aging the same way.
insights.locator: Each sensor model or each sensor will age differently

insights.claim: The industry will not train an individual AI model per vehicle — one model serves the entire fleet on a given software version, so that single model must absorb every distinct pattern of sensor degeneration across the fleet.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: The central architectural constraint of AV software: robustness to degraded inputs must be baked into training and validation, not patched per car — raises the bar on synthetic data and corner-case coverage tooling.
insights.quote: There will be one AI model for the fleet of vehicles with the same software version, and this AI model must deal with a lot of different ways of sensor degeneration.
insights.locator: So the real problem we are facing

insights.claim: Because AI outputs are probabilistic with a margin of error, tiny input variations can flip outcomes entirely — a single changed pixel on a camera image can cause a 30 mph sign to be read as 80 mph.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Small analog degradation maps to large semantic errors, which is why sensor aging is a safety problem rather than a gradual performance taper.
insights.quote: It might be one pixel changed on an on-camera image, leading to the effect that a 30 miles-per-hour sign is detected as 80 miles-per-hour.
insights.locator: But there’s always a margin of error

insights.claim: Sensor degeneration has to be modeled during development and folded into the safety analysis and the operational design domain, including defining what happens when specific pixels die and whether synthetic training data can be created for those failure modes.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: ODD definitions that ignore aging are incomplete; expect regulators and Tier 1s to demand degradation-aware safety cases, a new spend line for simulation and validation vendors.
insights.quote: we have to take it into consideration in our safety analysis and build our operational design domain around this consideration
insights.locator: Sensor degradation must be modeled into AI systems

insights.claim: The key unanswered question framed by Keysight is how sensor degeneration changes the 'safe interval of trust' — i.e., how long a system's outputs can be relied upon before revalidation, rather than whether the system works at time zero.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A shift from one-time homologation to periodic revalidation would create a recurring-revenue test and certification market.
insights.quote: how does the degeneration change the safe interval of trust?
insights.locator: We must define what happens if certain pixels die

insights.claim: AI has replaced the clear, inspectable decision path of classical algorithms with a black box, forcing safety cases and statistical analyses as the only route to a defensible confidence level about system safety.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Statistical safety argumentation is now the gating cost of AV deployment — it scales with miles and scenarios, not with headcount, favoring simulation-heavy players.
insights.quote: Now it’s abstracted to a black box, and this is why we have to go through the hassle of safety cases and statistical analyses
insights.locator: Previously, you had a clear decision path

insights.claim: Solving degradation-aware perception requires semiconductor manufacturer engineers, software makers and AI engineers to jointly share how models degrade, so the aging problem cannot be solved inside any one company's stack.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Points to consortium/standards formation as the next step — early participants gain data advantages that are hard to replicate later.
insights.quote: Semiconductor manufacturer engineers, software manufacturers, and AI engineers have to work together to share how models degrade
insights.locator: Getting inside that black box

insights.claim: AI can continuously analyze telemetry — vibration, temperature and output fluctuations — to detect micro-anomalies and flag degradation before a sensor actually fails, turning aging from a post-mortem into a predictive signal.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Predictive sensor-health analytics is an emerging attach-rate product for IP and EDA vendors selling into automotive.
insights.quote: AI can provide continuous analysis of telemetry, including vibrations, temperature, and output fluctuations to detect micro-anomalies, allowing systems to flag degradation ahead of sensor failure
insights.locator: Tracking sensor health

insights.claim: The incumbent technique for tracking silicon aging is on-chip monitors such as ring oscillators that measure how circuit timing shifts over life; SDVs are layering on calibration-drift and output-drift tracking on top of that baseline.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: On-chip monitoring IP moves from optional yield tooling to a shipped safety feature — a content-per-chip increase for silicon lifecycle management vendors.
insights.quote: on-chip aging monitors such as ring oscillators and similar structures that track how circuit timing shifts over life
insights.locator: The typical practice incorporates on-chip aging monitors

insights.claim: Degradation does not show up as a linear function in sensor readings and its profile varies by what is measured and where in the design, so producing an accurate health score with a remaining-days-to-failure estimate requires a very complex mathematical model.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Simple threshold-based health monitoring will not deliver credible RUL numbers — the modeling difficulty is the moat for whoever gets fleet-scale data first.
insights.quote: degradation does not always show up as a linear function in the sensor readings, and the profile can be very different depending on what is being measured and where in the design
insights.locator: The challenge comes from the fact that degradation

insights.claim: AI could learn the silicon lifecycle model from a deployment of several hundred thousand devices — Siemens EDA explicitly cites data-center fleets as the training ground — implying data-center scale is the path to automotive-grade aging models.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Whoever owns large fielded silicon fleets accumulates a proprietary aging dataset that transfers into automotive — a data flywheel argument for hyperscaler-adjacent EDA offerings.
insights.quote: it could potentially learn from a deployment of, say, several hundred thousand devices in a data center to build its own accurate model of the silicon lifecycle
insights.locator: This is an area where AI can be used

insights.claim: Rather than retiring silicon at a given health threshold, aging data can be used to schedule degraded parts onto smaller, less-intensive, non-critical tasks while keeping them out of high-load critical work — extending usable life instead of forcing replacement.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Health-aware workload placement lengthens silicon replacement cycles — a headwind to refresh-driven unit demand and a tailwind to lifecycle-analytics software.
insights.quote: instead of retiring all silicon that is running at, say, 25% health, the data could be used to ensure that the degrading silicon is not used to run any high-load critical tasks, but is reserved for smaller, less-intensive tasks
insights.locator: This data can also be used to aid deployment

insights.claim: Effective aging detection needs many data points because engineers must distinguish local from global degradation on a device, and aging traces back to multiple causes including thermal variation, high power and high switching factor.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Argues for dense on-die sensor arrays rather than a single monitor — more silicon area sold per design for monitoring IP.
insights.quote: More data points are better because one also needs to understand if the impact is local versus global on a device
insights.locator: With thin margins for error

insights.claim: Edge AI enables connecting multiple sensor types for a holistic view of vehicle operation rather than reading single sensors in isolation, with the industry starting on physically adjacent sensors to keep compute local before scaling to whole-car correlation.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A staged roadmap: near-term products are module-level multi-sensor blocks; whole-vehicle health correlation is the later, larger opportunity.
insights.quote: Initially, the industry is focused on connecting sensors that are close to each other to focus the compute to small regions, but we see possibilities for much greater insights.
insights.locator: Edge AI has also expanded the data tracking

insights.claim: A prematurely aged sensor can feed inaccurate data into safety-critical decisions, producing degraded object detection, incorrect sensor fusion or unsafe vehicle behavior — drift in a sensor propagates directly into dangerous AI decisions.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Input-validity checking becomes a required ADAS function; systems that cannot detect their own drifting inputs carry latent liability.
insights.quote: Safety systems are only as good as the data that feeds them
insights.locator: Keeping sensor data protected

themes.theme: Safety cost, redundancy, and single points of failure

insights.claim: Implementing a safety system is ultimately much more expensive than implementing a consumer-grade system, and AI-driven aging increases fault rates — so more fault detection and more redundancy must be designed in, raising the count of safe components inside the SoC.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Automotive AI silicon carries structurally worse cost-per-TOPS than consumer parts; margin models that extrapolate from consumer AI chips will be wrong.
insights.quote: Safety is expensive, so implementing a safety system is ultimately going to be much more expensive than implementing a consumer-grade system
insights.locator: But ensuring everything is working properly

insights.claim: Electrification is driving centralization of vehicle architecture, concentrating processing onto fewer devices, which turns those devices into single points of failure and forces redundancy back into the design.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: The zonal/central-compute consolidation thesis has a cost offset — fewer ECUs but far more expensive, redundancy-laden ones.
insights.quote: as electrification drives centralization of the vehicle architecture, more processing is done on fewer devices in the car, so those devices are becoming single points of failure
insights.locator: On the other hand, as electrification drives

insights.claim: The old partition where only the CPU and NPU needed functional safety no longer holds because safety-relevant workloads now run on the GPU too, so increasingly more of the SoC must be safety certified, possibly to ASIL-D or higher.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Certified-GPU IP becomes a gating requirement in automotive sockets — a share shift toward IP vendors that already carry ASIL-D-capable GPU and NPU portfolios, and a barrier for consumer-derived silicon.
insights.quote: Increasingly, more of the SoC is going to be safety certified, maybe up to ASIL-D, maybe even higher.
insights.locator: You’re also not going to be able to say

insights.claim: In a BEV or PHEV, a battery-management fault that trips the high-voltage pyrofuse stops the car dead and can disable safety-critical systems — an availability failure mode gasoline vehicles do not have.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Power-path availability is an under-discussed AV safety dependency; connects EV power semiconductor content to autonomy readiness.
insights.quote: in a BEV or PHEV the car will stop dead if there’s a problem in the battery management system, potentially disabling any safety-critical systems
insights.locator: Systems need to function as expected

insights.claim: Infineon argues the automotive pyrofuse should be replaced by a circuit breaker, because a blown pyrofuse destroys itself and requires a garage visit whereas a breaker protects without destruction — a recoverable-protection design shift.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A concrete product-replacement cycle in EV high-voltage protection — watch semiconductor-based HV circuit breakers displacing pyrotechnic fuses in BEV platforms.
insights.quote: The problem is, if it blows up, you have to bring your car to the garage to fix it
insights.locator: Typically, the battery protection is a pyrofuse

insights.claim: Infineon's stated position is that trust must be built by improving both the sensor and the perception AI simultaneously, and that today's cars are explicitly not yet the cars the industry wants to have in the future.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A major automotive supplier publicly framing current vehicles as an interim product supports continued sensor and compute content growth per vehicle.
insights.quote: we need to drive innovation forward, because the cars we have today are not yet those cars we really want to have in the future
insights.locator: There is still much work to be done

themes.theme: Designing silicon for workloads that don't exist yet

insights.claim: The shift to LLMs and transformer models over the last three to five years has pushed the performance requirements of autonomy processing through the roof, invalidating the compute-sizing assumptions of automotive SoCs designed before that shift.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Automotive compute designed pre-transformer is under-provisioned; explains the accelerated refresh cycle in ADAS SoC platforms.
insights.quote: the shift to LLMs and transformer models that have cropped up in the last three to five years has pushed the performance requirements of processing these large models through the roof
insights.locator: When you’re looking at AI computation

insights.claim: There is a hard economic ceiling on speculative silicon headroom — you can only put so much extra processing into an SoC before requirements materialize before it becomes cost-prohibitive, so automotive chip design is explicitly a bet on where applications will be years later.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Frames automotive AI silicon as an options-pricing problem; vendors that mis-bet face either uncompetitive BOM cost or stranded platforms mid-lifecycle.
insights.quote: there’s only so much more processing you can put into an SoC speculatively before the requirements are there, because it becomes cost-prohibitive
insights.locator: That’s a very hard thing to account for

insights.claim: Customers still deploying large amounts of NPU are now adding GPU processing for AI and signal-processing workloads specifically because the GPU's programmable, massively parallel flexibility hedges against not knowing future workloads.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Directional share shift from fixed-function NPU toward programmable GPU content in automotive SoCs — a positive read for GPU IP licensors targeting auto.
insights.quote: they’re adding GPU processing to cover some of this AI compute, or signal processing type of compute, so they can get sufficient performance even when they don’t know exactly what the workloads are going to be
insights.locator: A lot of our customers are thinking they need

insights.claim: Arm's position is that automotive hardware must be designed to support continuous software and AI model updates long after the vehicle leaves the factory, reframing the design problem from how silicon ages to how models and workloads evolve over the same period.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Update-capable compute headroom becomes a spec-level requirement in automotive RFQs, not a differentiator — raises the floor on silicon content per vehicle.
insights.quote: Hardware must be designed to support continuous software and AI updates long after a vehicle leaves the factory.
insights.locator: Keeping pace with AI

insights.claim: Arm argues general-purpose CPUs earn their place in AI vehicles as a stable execution platform that can run AI workloads directly or act as a fallback alongside dedicated AI accelerators, positioning the CPU as the degradation-and-obsolescence insurance policy.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A defensive argument for CPU content share against accelerator-only architectures — watch whether OEMs actually pay for redundant CPU headroom.
insights.quote: General-purpose CPUs play an important role by providing a stable execution platform that can continue running AI workloads directly, or serve as a fallback alongside dedicated AI accelerators.
insights.locator: Hardware must be designed to support continuous

insights.claim: Engineers building automotive AI models may not have a clear picture of how those models will stress the underlying hardware, particularly as models are updated over the air and learn on their own — creating a feedback loop where software evolution silently changes hardware aging.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Software and hardware reliability teams are decoupled today; the org that closes that loop first gets a real validation advantage.
insights.locator: Engineers developing AI models that will manage

themes.theme: Fleet telemetry, golden data, and drift attestation

insights.claim: Tesla's fine print permits extensive non-personally-identifying telemetry collection that is fed directly into its models to upgrade algorithms — Synopsys frames it as Google Maps or Waze mechanics applied to driving models rather than to traffic.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Fleet telemetry is the raw material for aging-aware model retraining; scale of installed fleet becomes a durable AV data moat.
insights.quote: They collect it all, then they upgrade their algorithm. It’s almost like Google Maps or Waze.
insights.locator: In the case of Tesla, if you read through the fine print

insights.claim: Synopsys expects a lot more pre-vetted 'golden data' to emerge and potentially be shared between companies, serving as a measurement baseline for detecting injected false data and material model drift.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Cross-company reference datasets would become shared infrastructure — an early standards/consortium play and a potential moat-eroder for data-advantaged incumbents.
insights.quote: We expect there will be a lot more golden data that’s pre-vetted and maybe even shared between companies
insights.locator: Securing these systems is another challenge

insights.claim: Synopsys argues AI systems must move from projecting reliability at design time to adapting over a lifetime, requiring more complex cross-layer trust correlation so that model behavior stays consistent rather than merely correct at launch.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Reframes automotive security IP from a static design-time feature to a lifetime service — supports recurring-revenue security software attached to silicon.
insights.quote: AI systems make it more important than ever to move from projecting at design time to adapting over a lifetime.
insights.locator: AI and sensor aging impact on automotive security

insights.claim: Model-drift defense requires signed updates, secure boot, code review and vulnerability management plus continuous attestation that no drift has occurred in the model, and Synopsys states plainly that existing methods are not enough going forward.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: An explicit gap statement from a security IP vendor — signals product roadmap and budget expansion in automotive AI lifecycle security and data provenance tooling.
insights.quote: There are methods today, but I don’t think that they’re enough for moving forward.
insights.locator: If they have methods for monitoring the drift

insights.claim: AI introduces non-deterministic aging in which accuracy degradation itself becomes a security vulnerability rather than merely a performance loss — a category of risk that classical automotive reliability engineering does not model.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Merges the reliability and security budgets in automotive; expands the security IP TAM into territory previously owned by functional-safety spending.
insights.quote: AI introduces some new concepts, including the non-deterministic type of aging, meaning there is some accuracy degradation that may become a security vulnerability, not just performance loss
insights.locator: AI and sensor aging impact on automotive security

insights.claim: Maliciously tampering with an analog sensor signal lets downstream digital processing amplify the bad behavior, making perception attacks on the analog side a distinct threat class from conventional digital cyberattacks.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Analog-domain security is a named blind spot — an unserved niche where new IP or startup entry is likely.
insights.quote: If the analog signal is maliciously tampered with from the digital side, you can really amplify the effect
insights.locator: Widespread adoption of ADAS and AV systems

insights.claim: Sensor fusion needs to be redesigned to be attack-aware — assuming adversarial inputs are possible rather than relying only on redundancy — because redundant sensors can be fooled together by a coordinated perception attack.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Redundancy-only safety architectures may not satisfy future security requirements; a design-requirement change that favors fusion-algorithm vendors.
insights.quote: so you don’t only focus on the redundancy, but the fusion that also can assume some adversarial attacks may be possible
insights.locator: Are there improved methods for more attack-aware

insights.claim: Synopsys states that security for the analog domain is very complex and that analog-side security considerations need to be investigated better than what is being done today — an explicit admission of an unaddressed vulnerability in shipping vehicles.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A named, currently unmitigated attack surface in mass-market ADAS — headline risk for OEMs if a real-world perception attack is demonstrated.
insights.quote: Security considerations need to be investigated from the analog side better than what is being done today.
insights.locator: With analog, it’s more of a perception kind of attack
